meeting_header:
Date: 2026-03-28
Time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Lucas Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Desai (Aurum AI - Head of AI), Tom Reynolds (Aurum - Platform), Sofia Martell (Aurum - CTO)
summary: Exploratory call to map integration surface for Aurum's multitenant inference gateway. Main concerns: routing through a proxy/gateway, SDK/Orchestration with LangChain and LlamaIndex, rate limiting and quota enforcement, and observability hooks for token-level cost and latency SLOs. Redwood to share examples and run a short benchmark.
topics: Rate limits and quota enforcement patterns
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:00:05] Priya (Aurum): Priya here.
[00:00:07] Tom: Tom here.
[00:00:09] Sofia: Sofia here.
[00:00:12] Lucas (Redwood SE): Lucas on the call as well.
[00:00:15] Maya: Great. High level agenda: we want to understand your integration needs — SDKs, whether you're planning a gateway/proxy, how you'll enforce quotas and rate limits, and what you need for observability. Priya, do you want to give 2 minutes on your context?
[00:00:30] Priya: Sure. We're building a customer-facing AI assistant that does document Q&A and generative summaries. Right now it's on an internal cluster using a mix of off‑the‑shelf models. We're evaling Redwood for hosted latency but also considering Dedicated or Private because some customers need data residency and tighter control. Key problems: we need a single ingress that routes traffic to different models, enforces quotas per‑customer, and gives us token level cost so billing ties back to accounts. Also want to reuse LangChain and LlamaIndex in our pipeline.
[00:01:06] Maya: Perfect. Quick clarifying Q — when you say single ingress, do you mean a customer facing gateway in front of Redwood, or we host the gateway?
[00:01:16] Tom: We're thinking of an edge proxy that we control — so requests hit our API gateway, then call Redwood endpoints. But we want Redwood to help with routing rules and fallback models when capacity is constrained.
[00:01:28] Lucas: Ok. Two patterns we commonly see: 1) proxy-as-traffic-router where your gateway routes to Redwood hosted endpoints by model tag; or 2) sidecar approach where Redwood client libs live inside your runtime and call local inference when private. The proxy approach is easiest for lots of customers and centralizes quotas. Sidecar/dedicated is better for private or on‑prem.
[00:01:50] Priya: For multitenancy the proxy seems cleaner. But we need per-tenant quotas, e.g., 100k tokens/month for free tier, and throttles at 10 tps for enterprise. How do you recommend implementing that?
[00:02:05] Lucas: You can do quota enforcement at the gateway layer, but Redwood also supports token-level billing and token quota enforcement via API keys and rate-limit headers. We emit header X-Redwood-Remaining-Tokens and also a per-request cost object in the response metadata — small note: response metadata is sometimes a little off in streaming responses, transcription says `resp meta` but it's present.
[00:02:25] Tom: Are those headers present for streaming and batch?
[00:02:28] Lucas: Yes, streaming includes periodic progress frames; each frame can include cumulative token cost in the metadata. For batch it's in the final response.
[00:02:35] Sofia: What about LangChain/LlamaIndex? Our orchestrator already runs LangChain chains and uses LlamaIndex for retrieval augmentation. We don't want to rework everything.
[00:02:45] Maya: We have SDKs and first-class connectors for both. Lucas, can you walk through the LangChain flow?
[00:02:50] Lucas: Sure. On LangChain we provide an LLM wrapper that implements the LLM API; it supports streaming, stop tokens, and function-calling. For LlamaIndex we have a connector that handles embedding calls and search indexing; note that some customers call LlamaIndex synchronously then fan-out to multiple models — that can increase token volume. Also worth noting: LlamaIndex sometimes shows up in transcripts as "Lama Index" or similar.
[00:03:15] Priya: Do you expose a single client key for all tenants or unique keys per tenant?
[00:03:20] Lucas: Unique keys per tenant are recommended. That lets you do per-API-key quotas and audit logs. If you want to centralize requests through one gateway key, we can still provide per-customer tagging in request metadata so you can split billing server-side, but it's more manual.
[00:03:34] Tom: Our other constraint is observability. We need traces that tie an app request to tokens consumed across multiple Redwood calls, and we want to see latency percentiles per-model per-route.
[00:03:44] Maya: Redwood Console exposes per-route/model dashboards with token and latency breakdowns. We also provide tracing headers so you can correlate with your tracing system — we support OpenTelemetry and emit spans for request lifecycle. Lucas, add the note about token-level cost export.
[00:03:58] Lucas: Right — there's an export option to push per-request metrics to your Prometheus or our metrics endpoint. For token-level cost export we provide a CSV/stream with fields: timestamp, api_key, model, prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, cost_usd. Small caveat: CSV may have a small delay for streaming responses.
[00:04:20] Priya: That delay — is it significant for billing? We need near real-time billing to prevent overages.
[00:04:27] Lucas: For strict enforcement you'd enforce quotas at the gateway; Redwood's exported billing metrics are best-effort near real-time, typically within a minute but can be longer under heavy load. So dual approach: enforce hard limits at gateway, use Redwood metrics for reconciliation.
[00:04:44] Sofia: On the networking side, if we go Dedicated or Private, how does routing change? We can't route through the public hosted endpoint.
[00:04:52] Maya: Dedicated gives you reserved capacity with a dedicated endpoint in our cloud; it still has a public endpoint but can be restricted by IP allowlist and VPC peering. Private gives you a private control plane and in some cases an on-prem package — that one is fully inside your network.
[00:05:08] Tom: For latency-sensitive flows we might want a local cache of KV work — is there a recommended pattern?
[00:05:13] Lucas: Yes, Redwood's runtime supports KV cache hints and prefix caching. Integration pattern: keep a lightweight local cache in your gateway for repeated prompt prefixes and enable Redwood's KV streaming to speed up cache warming. In transcripts KV cache sometimes transcribed as K V cache, but functionality is the same.
[00:05:30] Priya: Let's talk about fallbacks. We want to route to a cheaper quantized model during load but keep response quality high. Is that automatic?
[00:05:38] Maya: We offer smart routing policies. You define a primary model and fallback variants; the router can failover on latency or capacity thresholds. You can also configure percentage rollouts for canarying.
[00:05:49] Tom: What's the developer experience? How intrusive are SDK changes?
[00:05:53] Lucas: Minimal. Our SDK presents the same call surface across hosted, dedicated, and private. You configure endpoint and api_key. If you use LangChain, you swap the LLM wrapper. If you use LlamaIndex, swap the connector endpoint and set embeddings model name. The common friction is handling streaming semantics if your orchestrator expects sync responses.
[00:06:15] Priya: Any gotchas we should know integrating with our rate limiter (we use Envoy)?
[00:06:20] Lucas: Envoy is a common pattern. Two things: propagate client identity in headers so Redwood can attribute usage, and ensure Envoy's connection pooling doesn't buffer streaming frames too long. Some transcriptions show buffering issues as 'latency spikes' but it's really HTTP/2 flow control.
[00:06:36] Maya: We also recommend per-request timeouts and retries with exponential backoff. Redwood SDKs surface retry helpers.
[00:06:44] Sofia: Security — SSO, KMS, audit logs. We need SAML SSO for our enterprise admin console, keys stored in our HSM, and full audit logs for every request.
[00:06:53] Maya: We support SAML/SSO for the Console; for Dedicated/Private you can integrate your KMS/HSM. Audit logs are available with enterprise plans and can be forwarded to your SIEM. We'll include SOC2 and ISO docs in the follow up.
[00:07:08] Tom: Latency: our P95 needs to be under 400ms for 512 token responses. Can Redwood guarantee that?
[00:07:15] Lucas: SLAs depend on plan. Dedicated has tighter SLOs due to reserved GPU pools. Hosted is best-effort but we do have latency profiles in the model catalog. Still for 512 tokens, network adds variance; Dedicated with burst capacity is the safest bet to meet 400ms P95.
[00:07:32] Priya: Pricing: token costs and dedicated seat pricing?
[00:07:36] Maya: We'll send a matrix. High level: hosted is usage-based per token; dedicated is a monthly commitment with lower per-token costs and guaranteed throughput; private has license + support. I'll attach an example.
[00:07:47] Sofia: Ok. Can you run a bench using our real sample traffic?
[00:07:50] Maya: Yes. That would be our first POC. Lucas, we'll need a small test harness.
[00:07:56] Lucas: I'll prepare a LangChain example that replays your traces and a direct SDK harness for token accounting. Also include a gateway proxy example using Nginx/Envoy with per-tenant quotas.
[00:08:07] Priya: For the demo, we also want to see observability: token breakdown and per-route latency dashboards.
[00:08:12] Maya: We'll include a short walkthrough of Redwood Console and the OpenTelemetry integration.
[00:08:17] [crosstalk - 00:08:17 to 00:08:20] Tom: Perfect.
[00:08:21] Maya: Quick recap of next steps: send pricing and compliance docs, Lucas to share sample repos, Aurum to provide sample traces and token distribution, schedule benchmark next week. Anything else?
[00:08:34] Sofia: One ask — can you show how to limit function calls or chain depth from LangChain to control token usage?
[00:08:40] Lucas: Yes, we'll show examples with stop sequences and max tokens and a LangChain middleware that clamps chain depth.
[00:08:47] Priya: Great. That covers it.
[00:08:50] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the materials.
[00:08:54] [meeting ends quickly with some post-meeting chat and file links posted in chat: https://redwood.example.com/sdk-samples, https://redwood.example.com/security/soc2]
